LONDON, England (CNN) -- Former world number one Pete Sampras has described recently crowned French Open champion Roger Federer as the best player in history, after the Swiss star equalled Sampras’s record of 14 men’s singles Grand Slam titles.

The 37-year-old American, nicknamed “Pistol Pete” for his bullet-like serves, won a record 14 Grand Slam men’s singles titles over a 15-year career, though he never captured the trophy at Roland Garros.

By defeating Sweden’s Robin Soderling 6-1, 7-6, 6-4 to claim the French Open title on Sunday, Federer equalled Sampras’s record and became only the sixth man in history to win each of the four majors.

Debate: Is Federer the greatest player ever?

According to Sampras, the feat confirms the 27-year-old Swiss as the finest player ever to grace the game.

“What he’s done over the past five years has never, ever been done -- and probably will never, ever happen again.

“Regardless if he won there or not, he goes down as the greatest ever. This just confirms it,” Sampras told The Guardian newspaper.

“I’m obviously happy for Roger. If there’s anyone that deserves it, it’s Roger. He’s come so close previously,” Sampras said of the new champion and world number two, who had lost the previous three consecutive French Open finals to Spain’s Rafael Nadal.

Federer spoke exclusively to CNN after his win and said he was relieved to have bounced back after relinquishing the world number one ranking, as well as the Australian Open and Wimbledon titles, to Nadal in 2008.

“It’s been a fantastic day -- to get the elusive French title in the end was unbelievable. I always believed I was good enough to get it -- but holding the trophy, after all I’ve been through, was just unbelievable. I’m so proud right now, you can’t believe it.

“For me, there was never a question whether I was going to retire. I worked extremely hard in the off-season. Losing semifinals and finals all of a sudden wasn’t good enough for people anymore. But this victory is timely because I’ve proved many people wrong.”

The historic nature of the victory was also not lost on Federer.

“The records mean a lot to me, especially after the last few years, when I realized that I was up there with the greatest players of all time. Of course I like to break records -- because I look up to people like Sampras, Agassi, Connors and McEnroe, it’s so great to be up there with those players.”

However, in an ominous warning to his rivals, the champion said he already had his sights set on his next conquest.

“I still feel like I have much more left in me -- I’m only 27 years old, and I’d like to play for many more years to come. I hope I reach many more titles.”

Federer’s vanquished opponent in the final, Soderling, also praised his conqueror.

“For me, he is the best ever, and I should know, as I’ve played him many times,” the world number 12 told CNN.

Next up for Federer is the third Grand Slam of 2009, Wimbledon, where he will aim to go one better than Bjorn Borg by winning the tournament for a sixth time when the event starts on June 22.

Federer’s historic weekend win was recognized by International Olympic Committee president Jacques Rogge, who also described the Swiss as the best tennis has ever seen.

“Today I wrote to Roger Federer to congratulate him on this unique success because I consider him to be the best player of all time,” Rogge told a media briefing in Brussels on Monday.

The IOC president revealed that, in the letter, he had expressed the hope that Federer would take part in the 2012 Olympic Games in London.

Federer added an Olympic gold medal to his collection of tennis accolades by winning the men’s doubles with compatriot Stanislas Wawrinka in Beijing last year.

He added that retirement had never been on his mind.

“For me there was never a question whether I was going to retire. I worked extremely hard in the off season. Losing semifinals and finals all of a sudden wasn't good enough for people anymore. But this victory is timely because I've proved many people wrong.”

“The records mean a lot to me especially after the last few years when I realized that I was (up there) with the greatest players of all time. Federer’s triumph in France immediately shifted attention to Wimbledon, where he would arrive with renewed confidence and a chance to make even more history.

**Federer’s Paris breakthrough prompts “greatest ever” chorus from Sampras, Soderling and Rogge**

PARIS — Roger Federer’s first French Open title did more than fill the lone empty space in his trophy cabinet. It changed the terms of tennis history.

When Federer defeated Robin Soderling in the 2009 Roland Garros final, 6-1, 7-6, 6-4, he became only the sixth man at the time to complete the career Grand Slam — winning all four major championships. He also claimed his 14th Grand Slam singles title, equaling Pete Sampras’s men’s record. For many observers, that combination was decisive: Federer had matched the most important numerical benchmark in the sport while achieving something Sampras never did — conquering the clay of Paris.

That is why, in the immediate aftermath of Federer’s breakthrough, major figures including Sampras, Soderling and International Olympic Committee president Jacques Rogge viewed the Swiss as the greatest player tennis had seen.

### The missing title that changed the debate

Before Roland Garros 2009, Federer’s résumé was already extraordinary. He had won Wimbledon five times in a row, dominated the U.S. Open, captured multiple Australian Open titles and spent years as world No. 1. But one argument remained against him in the greatest-ever debate: he had not won the French Open.

That omission mattered because clay-court success has historically separated all-surface champions from fast-court specialists. Federer had reached three previous French Open finals, losing each time to Rafael Nadal, the dominant clay-court player of his era and one of the finest clay players in history. Those defeats were often used to question whether Federer could truly be placed above every champion before him.

The 2009 tournament removed that objection.

Nadal’s shock fourth-round defeat to Soderling opened the draw, but Federer still had to survive pressure, expectation and difficult matches of his own. He came through a five-set scare against Tommy Haas, beat Juan Martin del Potro in a demanding semifinal, and then handled Soderling in the final with the calm of a player determined not to let history escape him.

By the end of the match, Federer had joined an elite group of men to win all four majors — a feat achieved before him by Fred Perry, Don Budge, Rod Laver, Roy Emerson and Andre Agassi. In the modern era, with deeper fields, different surfaces and intense specialization, the achievement carried enormous weight.

### Sampras: the record-holder gives way

Pete Sampras’s view was especially significant because Federer had just tied his record of 14 Grand Slam titles. Sampras had long been the statistical standard in men’s tennis. His 14 majors, including seven Wimbledon titles, had stood as the benchmark Federer was chasing.

But Sampras had never won the French Open. He reached only one semifinal in Paris, in 1996, and clay remained the one surface on which his attacking game was least comfortable.

Federer’s victory therefore gave him a claim Sampras could not match: the same number of majors, but spread across every major tournament. To Sampras, that mattered. Federer had not merely equaled his record; he had done so with a broader range of achievements.

The reasoning was clear. If two players are tied on Grand Slam titles, the one who has won all four majors holds the more complete résumé. Federer had conquered grass, hard courts and clay. He had dominated his era, reached an extraordinary number of major finals, and now completed the career Grand Slam. For Sampras, that was enough to place Federer at the top of the historical conversation.

### Soderling: beaten finalist acknowledges the standard

Robin Soderling’s perspective carried a different kind of authority. He had just produced one of the biggest upsets in tennis history by defeating Nadal at Roland Garros — Nadal’s first loss at the tournament. Soderling then backed it up by reaching the final, proving his run was no fluke.

Yet against Federer, he was outplayed for much of the match. Federer’s variety was decisive: precise serving, clean forehand strikes, sharp movement, low backhand slices and deft net play. The final was not simply about Federer overpowering Soderling; it was about the full range of his game.

Soderling’s respect reflected what opponents often said about Federer at his peak: he could beat players in multiple ways. He could attack, defend, absorb pace, change rhythm and expose weaknesses with subtle tactical shifts. Against a big-hitting opponent who had just taken out Nadal, Federer made the final feel controlled.

For Soderling, Federer’s greatness was not an abstract historical argument. It was something experienced across the net. Having seen firsthand how Federer handled the biggest match of his clay-court career, Soderling recognized the scale of the player he had lost to.

### Rogge: greatness beyond tennis statistics

Jacques Rogge’s admiration also showed that Federer’s achievement resonated beyond the tennis world. As president of the International Olympic Committee, Rogge represented the broader sporting establishment, and Federer’s victory fit the Olympic ideal of sustained excellence, grace under pressure and international stature.

Federer was already one of sport’s most recognizable figures. He had won Olympic gold in doubles with Switzerland in 2008, carried himself with a polished global image and was widely regarded as an ambassador for tennis. The French Open title enhanced that standing because it completed the portrait of an all-court champion.

To Rogge and other international sports leaders, Federer’s greatness was not just about counting trophies. It was about the manner of his dominance: consistency, elegance, sportsmanship and the ability to perform across countries, surfaces and eras of expectation.

### Why the 2009 French Open was the turning point

Federer’s first Roland Garros title became a turning point because it answered the last major criticism of his career. Before Paris, skeptics could say he was the greatest grass-court and hard-court player of his generation but not a complete champion. After Paris, that argument weakened dramatically.

The case for Federer as the greatest ever rested on several pillars:

- **He had tied Sampras’s men’s record of 14 Grand Slam titles.**
- **He had completed the career Grand Slam.**
- **He had reached repeated French Open finals during Nadal’s clay-court reign.**
- **He had shown dominance on grass, hard courts and clay.**
- **He had sustained excellence over many seasons as world No. 1.**
- **He combined statistical success with a style of play widely admired for its variety and elegance.**

The emotional weight of the moment was also important. Federer had been burdened by near-misses in Paris, and his tears after victory reflected the release of years of pressure. It was not just another major title; it was the title that made his record feel complete.

### A debate that evolved, but a moment that mattered

Tennis’s greatest-ever debate has continued to evolve, especially with the later achievements of Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic. But in June 2009, Federer’s claim was stronger than it had ever been. He had matched Sampras’s record and surpassed him in all-surface completeness. He had earned the respect of the man he beat in the final. And he had impressed leading figures in world sport such as Rogge.

For Sampras, Soderling and Rogge, Federer’s French Open triumph was the final piece of evidence. It transformed him from a dominant champion with one missing line on his résumé into a complete champion whose achievements spanned the whole geography of tennis.

On that Paris afternoon, the argument was simple: Roger Federer had won everything that mattered. And for many, that made him the greatest ever.
